item.title: Sixteen countries back sanctions targeting Israel’s illegal settlement expansion
item.description:
Sixteen countries back sanctions targeting Israel’s illegal settlement expansion

Submitted by Elis Gjevori on Fri, 11/20/2026 - 12:14
Joint statement welcomes measures against settlement firms and an Israeli settler group blocking humanitarian aid to Gaza
Israeli settlers who want to occupy Gaza in a field outside Kibbutz Nir-Am by the Israel-Gaza boundary on 27 September 2026 (Ilia Yefimovich/AFP)
Off

Sixteen Muslim-majority countries have welcomed decisions by the UK and Australia to impose sanctions over Israel’s illegal settlement activities in occupied Palestine.

In a joint statement, foreign ministers from major countries including Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Algeria said the sanctions came "in response to illegal Israeli settlement activities in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including measures targeting companies involved in settlement construction".

They also welcomed the UK’s decision to sanction an organisation obstructing humanitarian aid deliveries to Gaza.

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced the sanctions on Tuesday, shortly before the Israeli government was scheduled to allocate tenders for the E1 settlement bloc, which would effectively split the occupied West Bank in two.

Hours after the announcement, Israel postponed the issuing of tenders for construction in the E1 settlement in the West Bank until a new government is formed. Israeli officials insisted the decision was not in response to the sanctions.

The sanctions target eight Israeli construction, property development and architectural firms.

The UK also sanctioned Tsav9, an Israeli group involved in blocking aid deliveries into Gaza. The United States sanctioned the group in 2024.

The Foreign Office described Tsav9 as "an Israeli activist movement whose stated mission has been to stop humanitarian aid entering the Gaza Strip, and which has organised and carried out blockades of crossings, ports and roads used by humanitarian aid convoys bound for Gaza".

The foreign ministers said they "express support for all efforts to ensure accountability, including through appropriate international measures and the imposition of sanctions on entities and individuals responsible for settlement activities, including the E1 settlement plan, as well as those that support, facilitate or implement settlement expansion and annexation policies".

"The Ministers renew their strongest condemnation of Israel’s continued settlement policies in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, particularly the 'E1' settlement plan and related settlement activities east of occupied East Jerusalem. They express the hope that this decision by the UK and Australia would encourage many in the international community to follow suit," the statement added.

UK imposes sanctions on eight Israeli firms and a group blocking Gaza aid
Read More »

Other signatories included Palestine, Jordan, Indonesia, Niger, Libya, the Maldives, Somalia and Kuwait.

The ministers also condemned Israel’s ongoing "military escalation in Gaza and called for the full and immediate implementation of President Trump’s Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict, to ensure security and stability, address the humanitarian situation, facilitate reconstruction and recovery, and lay the foundations for lasting peace".

Explaining his decision, Miliband said: "Protecting the two-state solution is the north star of this government’s approach. That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.

"And we will not stand by while those blocking desperately needed aid deepen the intolerable suffering of civilians in Gaza. The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable."

Miliband also said the UK was "committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike".

The Foreign Office has published a list of the Israeli companies sanctioned on Tuesday.

item.title: Israeli experts warn Myanmar genocide ruling could strengthen Gaza case at ICJ
item.description:
Israeli experts warn Myanmar genocide ruling could strengthen Gaza case at ICJ

Submitted by Nadav Rapaport on Fri, 11/20/2026 - 12:48
Israeli officials and legal experts fear the International Court of Justice's landmark ruling could influence its eventual judgment on South Africa's genocide case against Israel
Displaced Palestinians living in tents set up among the rubble of their destroyed homes in Jabalia, northern Gaza Strip (Salah Hashem/ZUMA Press Wire via Reuters)
Off

Thursday's landmark ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), holding Myanmar responsible for genocide against its Rohingya minority, has raised alarm among Israeli officials and legal experts over its potential implications for the genocide case against Israel over Gaza.

"This is a dangerous precedent," a senior Israeli official told Ynet, referring to the ruling, which marked the first time the ICJ had found a state responsible for committing genocide.

"This sets parameters and standards that, admittedly, you can't apply one-to-one to Israel, but it opens the door," the official added. While Israel's case in Gaza is "more complicated", the ruling "certainly doesn't do us any good".

Another Israeli official told the public broadcaster Kan 11 that the decision reflected "worrying trends" at the top UN court, but insisted Israel could avoid a similar ruling in the case brought by South Africa in December 2023.

The official said Israel could withstand "any legal test", insisting that "we did not commit a genocide". They estimated that a final judgment in the Gaza genocide case would not be delivered before 2030.

Since October 2023, when Israel launched its military onslaught on the Gaza Strip following the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October, UN officials, genocide experts and humanitarian organisations have accused Israel of committing genocide in the besieged enclave.

Since then, the Israeli army has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, most of them children, women and elderly people. Israel has also used starvation as a weapon, depriving Palestinians of basic necessities, while air strikes and bulldozers have devastated much of Gaza's built environment.

'Israel must prepare'

Israeli legal experts who spoke to Ynet echoed officials' concerns about the potential implications of Thursday's ruling for Israel.

Yuval Shany, an international law expert at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, told the outlet that the ICJ ruling "should worry Israel", arguing that the court had changed "the method by which acts of genocide are proven".

Shany said the decision signalled a shift towards "a holistic examination of all the circumstances and the only reasonable conclusion that can be drawn from them".

"There is also a greater willingness to view harm that does not involve loss of life as part of the elements of the offence," he added.

Alan Baker, director of the Institute for Diplomatic Affairs at the Jerusalem Centre for Security and Foreign Affairs, an Israeli research group, dismissed South Africa's genocide accusations against Israel but said the ruling was nevertheless concerning.

"Political considerations and the atmosphere in the international arena could influence how the case against Israel is examined in the future," Baker said, adding that "Israel must prepare for this legally and diplomatically".

'For Israel, the central issue is how the court examined the specific intent required for genocide'

- Tammy Caner, head of the Law and National Security Programme at INSS

Tammy Caner, head of the Law and National Security Programme at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), told Ynet that the court's decision could have far-reaching consequences for Israel.

"For the first time, the International Court of Justice has determined that a state bears direct responsibility for committing genocide," she said, adding that "for Israel, the central issue is how the court examined the specific intent required for genocide".

The practical implication for Israel, Caner said, was that presenting its military objective of eliminating Hamas would not, in itself, be enough to rule out genocidal intent.

The INSS expert also noted that ICJ judges had emphasised states' obligations to prevent genocide, including investigating reported crimes and holding those responsible accountable.

"From Israel's perspective," she said, the ruling underscored "the importance of taking effective preventive and enforcement measures and documenting them".

item.title: Exclusive: UAE's Nusseibeh lobbied UK's Iain Duncan Smith over UN candidacy
item.description:
Exclusive: UAE's Nusseibeh lobbied UK's Iain Duncan Smith over UN candidacy

Submitted by Oscar Rickett on Fri, 11/20/2026 - 11:20
The former Conservative leader told the Emirati diplomat that the UAE had to 'cease and desist' from its involvement in the Sudan war and release imprisoned British citizens
Former Conservative Party leader Iain Duncan Smith pictured in 2019 (AFP)
Off

Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh visited former Conservative Party leader Iain Duncan Smith at his office in the UK’s Houses of Parliament to lobby him over her candidacy for UN secretary-general, Middle East Eye can reveal.

Nusseibeh visited just over two weeks ago after Duncan Smith spoke out in parliament about the UAE’s “sponsoring of a huge amount of terrorism in Sudan” and called on the British government to use its Security Council veto to block her nomination.

The former government minister told MEE that in his meeting with Nusseibeh he reiterated the position he had taken in parliament about the UAE’s involvement in Sudan - denied by Abu Dhabi - and called for the release of “two British citizens wrongly held in Dubai: Ryan Cornelius and Charles Ridley”.

Duncan Smith told Nusseibeh that the UAE needed to “cease and desist” from its involvement in the Sudan war, where Abu Dhabi has sponsored the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary force found to have committed genocide in Darfur by the UN and US.

He told Nusseibeh that her UN candidacy gave the UAE a chance to do the right thing and withdraw from the war in Sudan and release Cornelius and Ridley, two British citizens who have been detained in Dubai for almost 20 years.

The British politician said that in their meeting, Nusseibeh, who was the Emirati ambassador to the UN from 2013 to 2024, did not deny that the UAE was involved in Sudan's war.

“She didn’t really say very much. She didn’t try and pretend they weren’t involved,” he said. Instead, “she said she wanted to be independent. I said you are not seen as independent. You are party to this barbarity”. 

When asked if she would disavow the UAE, Duncan Smith said she told him she worked for the Emirati foreign ministry.

“It’s not my problem if you are part of the foreign ministry… if you are a member of the foreign ministry, you aren’t impartial,” the former Tory leader said in response, adding that when he disagreed with his government, he resigned.

In 2016, Duncan Smith resigned as work and pensions secretary, citing pressure to cut disability benefits.

'She said she wanted to be independent. I said you are not seen as independent. You are party to this barbarity'

- Iain Duncan Smith, British MP

“She was very personable. It was all polite,” Duncan Smith said. “I was even impressed that she bothered to talk to me.”

A spokesperson for Nusseibeh’s campaign told MEE: “Lana Nusseibeh is meeting a wide range of stakeholders as part of her candidacy for UN secretary-general.

"We do not comment on the content of private meetings. Lana has taken a leave of absence from her ministerial role since the submission of her nomination. She took this decision as part of her genuine commitment to the independence of her campaign and potential future role.”

The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF, which has been at war with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) since April 2023. The SAF receives military backing from Turkey and Egypt.

Race for the UN's top job

Born in Abu Dhabi into a famous Palestinian family, Nusseibeh was educated at an English boarding school and the University of Cambridge. She is well regarded by many who have worked with her.

“She’s the best diplomat I’ve ever met… She's charming. She's extremely eloquent. She's a fast thinker,” one former British diplomat said.

"She's assertive, and so she’s been good at articulating the UAE’s foreign policy position, which is that it has a right to be assertive."

'The Treasury is the most powerful department in government, and the issue is that they are panic stricken that this wealthy country will not invest in the UK'

- Iain Duncan Smith, British MP

But her bid to succeed Antonio Guterres, whose term ends on 31 December, has been mired in controversy over her government’s involvement in Sudan. UN Panel of Experts reports have confirmed that the UAE is supplying the RSF with weapons and mercenaries.

In her role as an Emirati diplomat, Nusseibeh has dismissed the findings of prior Panel of Experts reports and lobbied members of the European Parliament to remove the words “United Arab Emirates” from a resolution on the war in Sudan.

There are eight candidates for the UN’s top job, with the next straw poll - an informal, anonymous poll on whether members encourage, discourage or have no opinion about a candidate – expected to take place on Friday after being postponed from Thursday.

Candidates need to secure nine “approve” votes from the Security Council's 15 members. Crucially, they must ensure that none of the “disapprove” votes come from its five permanent members, known as the P5, each of which holds a veto.

The UK is one of the P5, along with the US, Russia, France and China.

Diplomatic sources previously told MEE that China - despite selling drones used in Sudan to Abu Dhabi - was the country most likely to veto Nusseibeh’s candidacy. She met Zeng Jixin, China’s ambassador to the UAE, on Thursday.

The UAE's 'money and investment'

The UAE has a population of around 11 million, just over one million of whom are Emirati citizens. Despite its size, it has used its vast wealth - originally derived from oil and gas exports - to project power across the Middle East and into Africa while developing significant economic ties with every P5 member.

Duncan Smith told MEE that Emirati investment in the UK is extremely significant to Britain’s position on Nusseibeh’s candidacy. 

This includes a commitment to invest almost $30bn between 2021 and 2026 through the UAE-UK Sovereign Investment Partnership, as well as Manchester City Football Club and significant real estate projects in Manchester and London,

'What I would say to Ed Miliband is that this is the moment to take a stand'

- Iain Duncan Smith, British MP

The Treasury - the British government's economic and finance ministry, which controls public spending and sets the direction of UK economic policy - “will say we need the Emiratis”, Duncan Smith said.

“And the Treasury is the most powerful department in government, and the issue is that they are panic-stricken that this wealthy country will not invest in the UK.”

“I think the leverage the UAE has over the UK is mainly down to money and investment,” a former British official, who worked on securing Emirati investment in the UK while in government, told MEE.

“They are a security partner and seen as a stable balancing state in the Middle East,” the source said. “But they are not as strategically important as Oman or Saudi Arabia.”

“They are corrupt, and they are corrupting,” Duncan Smith said of the Emiratis. “What I would say to Ed Miliband is that this is the moment to take a stand.”

British citizens imprisoned in Dubai

Duncan Smith has campaigned for years for the release of Charles Ridley and Ryan Cornelius.

Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary, has met Cornelius’s family.

Cornelius, a British property developer, has been imprisoned in Dubai since 2008 over bank fraud allegations. Ridley, also a British businessman, is serving a 20-year sentence for fraud. 

The UN has called both men’s detention arbitrary and called for their release.

Mohammed al-Shaibani, a long-term confidante of Dubai's ruler, Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, has been accused of using his former position as chairman of Dubai Islamic Bank to ensure Cornelius’s continued imprisonment. He recently resigned from that role and has reportedly been stripped of all his duties in the emirate.

Nusseibeh has given a series of interviews to major western publications as part of her UN campaign. Commenting on a meeting she held with Massad Boulos, the US adviser for Arab and African affairs, the Emirati diplomat said that as UN secretary-general, ending the war in Sudan would be “my focus from day one”. 

“In my first 100 days, I will work to protect civilians, secure humanitarian access, and support a political process,” she said. “The people of Sudan have waited long enough. Peace cannot wait.”

UK Politics
Peter Oborne
London

item.title: Japan agrees to buy up to 8M barrels of Saudi crude to rebuild oil reserves
item.description: Japan has agreed to buy up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude for its national petroleum reserve if market conditions are favorable, the two countries said Friday, Anadolu reports. The agreement also expands the storage capacity available to Saudi Arabia in Japan. The kingdom, which already has access to 8 million barrels of capacity, will gain temporary use of storage for 16 million barrels, according to a joint statement carried by the Saudi Press Agency. Saudi Arabia has already begun replenishing crude stocks at storage facilities in Japan, the statement said. Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman and Japan’s Economy, Trade and Industry Minister Ryosei Akazawa reached the agreement during a virtual meeting.
